                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §              BEFORE THE
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                    §               OF TEXAS

               ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY’S COMMENTS
       ON COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) files these comments to the second Rule

25.194 discussion draft issued by the staff (“Staff”) of the Public Utility Commission of Texas

(“Commission”) on January 2, 2026 and in response to Staff’s invitation for comments issued in

the January 9, 2026, workshop. Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s efforts to

adopt new rules that implement Senate Bill 6.

               I.    COMMENTS ON RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT

1. Section (i)(9): Oncor reiterates its stance on CIAC for system upgrades – interconnecting
   customers should not be responsible for system upgrades because it stifles growth,
   introduces unnecessary complexity, and does not allocate costs based on current or future
   benefit.
       Oncor urges Staff to modify the CIAC provisions included in the second discussion draft.

As further discussed in Oncor’s prior comments on the first discussion draft filed in this docket

and in its comments filed in Docket No. 58484, Section (i)(9)’s imposition of system upgrade costs

on interconnecting large load customers would be a drastic change in the way the Commission

assigns transmission project costs that would create a first-mover problem and would likely stifle

economic growth in direct opposition to the express purposes of Senate Bill 6. Further, the draft

discussion version of Section (i)(9) would introduce onerous accounting and modeling

complexities that promise to create significant delays in the interconnection process. Finally, cost

causation principles support that the cost of networked assets should be shared by all users on the




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
Page 1 of 9
 system through transmission rates because these assets benefit the entirety of the system and each

of its users by definition.

        Deciding whether system upgrades “would not be required but for the interconnecting large

load customer” introduces significant modeling challenges that will likely delay both the

construction of new system upgrades and the interconnection of large loads – the rule would

require the interconnecting utility to determine which future system upgrades are “but-for”

upgrades and calculate the specific cost of these upgrades, which it will charge the customer as

CIAC, before beginning construction on system upgrades or the facilities required to directly

interconnect the large load. This creates a significant first-mover problem by placing all cost

responsibility of system upgrades that benefit the entire grid on the shoulders of a single,

incremental customer.         This misallocation causes cancellations and delays, as proven by

experience in other regional transmission operator (“RTO”) territories. The RTOs that have

implemented CIAC for transmission network upgrades in the new generation context (e.g.,

Southwest Power Pool and Midcontinent Independent System Operator) have been plagued with

project cancellations and multi-year interconnection delays for new generation projects.

        Reallocating responsibility for system upgrades when new large loads interconnect adds

another layer of unneeded complexity and delay. Section (h)(9)(C) directs the reallocation of

system upgrade costs to subsequent large load customers seeking interconnection. Oncor is not

aware of any method for allocating responsibility for system upgrades among multiple large load

customers based on usage or any other variable. The extent to which a given customer “uses” a

transmission asset cannot be conclusively modeled. Grid modeling examines the effects of

multiple contingencies and scenarios on how power could flow across the system. The directions

and magnitudes of power flows across the system vary widely depending on the modeled



ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
Page 2 of 9
 contingency or scenario. One contingency or scenario may result in a given large load “using”

nearly all the capacity of a system upgrade, while another may result in the load using none of the

upgrade’s capacity at all. And these determinations are bound to prove contentious and may result

in contested cases that delay the interconnection of many subsequent large loads for years.

           The complexities of determining “but-for” responsibility for system upgrades and

reallocating responsibility as new large load customers interconnect only multiply with any future

introduction of a batch study process. There is no reasonable way to discern which large load

customer included in a batch is the “but-for” cause of, and therefore should be responsible for, a

system upgrade when each of the large loads are modeled together in a single batch. And if

multiple large load customers in a batch are deemed “but-for” causes of a system upgrade, the

same allocation challenges described above will grind the construction of these new required

system upgrades to a halt.

       Networked assets, including those constructed as part of system upgrades, inherently

benefit the entirety of the Texas grid, not just the incremental customer whose interconnection

happens to trigger the need for a system upgrade. Oncor agrees that interconnecting customers

should be required to pay CIAC equal to the costs of direct interconnection facilities,1 the facilities

that will only be used by the interconnecting load. Any costs related to transmission facilities that

are used or could be used in the future by other customers should be system costs because of their

wider benefit. Please refer to Oncor’s Comments on Commission Staff’s Rule 25.194 Discussion

Draft filed in this docket on December 19, 2025, for further discussion regarding Oncor’s

recommended alternative language.




       1
           Subject to a utility tariff’s standard interconnection allowance.

ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
Page 3 of 9
 2. Section (d): the initial screening study language should be modified to (i) describe initial
   study results that are clear and realistic and (ii) leave room for a potential initial batch
   study process.
       Oncor recommends that the initial study process found in Section (d) of the Commission’s

second discussion draft be modified to require initial study results that are clear and realistic. The

existing language presumes that utilities conducting an initial study could produce an accurate and

actionable interconnection timeline within 30 days of the study request: “[i]f based on the initial

screening study, the interconnecting utility provides the large load customer with an

interconnection timeline of three years or more . . . .” This is not a realistic output of an initial,

30-day study. The only accurate outputs would be basic estimates of the availability of capacity

and the general level of upgrades necessary to interconnect a load at the requested site. An initial

study conducted by a utility would model the system as is; it could not reasonably factor in the

effect of the parallel requests for future interconnection submitted by other large load customers

in the immediate or surrounding service territories.

       Additionally, Oncor recommends that the Commission modify the latest discussion draft

to leave room for a future shift to an ERCOT-led initial batch study process. As ERCOT shifts

towards a centralized batch study process, it is likely that the batch study process that

simultaneously includes prospective large loads across the system would yield the most accurate

and detailed initial study. The rule should require the interconnecting utility to either complete a

utility-driven initial study or submit information necessary for inclusion of the large load customer

in an initial study to ERCOT within 30 days of executing the large load interconnection screening

agreement, whichever applicable.

3. The rule should require that, in instances where multiple utilities are involved, they are
   required to execute an agreement or agreements that divide responsibilities amongst the
   utilities.



ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
Page 4 of 9
         Oncor supports Staff’s effort to refine the definition of “interconnecting utility” such that

it rightfully contemplates scenarios where the retail utility is a different entity than the transmission

service provider. Oncor recommends that the Commission further modify the discussion draft to

require that utilities in these multi-utility scenarios execute an agreement that allocates relevant

critical interconnection responsibilities as the parties see fit.           The Commission should

appropriately accommodate the diversity of utility practices by not requiring a set allocation or the

inclusion of an allocation in a specific agreement. The Commission should allow utilities to

allocate responsibilities in either the large load interconnection study, intermediate, or

interconnection agreements, or in a separate agreement entirely. The agreement should include

the large load customer, the retail utility, and any transmission service providers and should at least

allocate responsibility for collection of financial security and CIAC, collection of required

customer disclosures, submission of large load forecasting data to ERCOT, management of any

initial study, management of the Large Load Interconnection Study (“LLIS”), and submission of

LLIS results to ERCOT.

4. Section (b)(9): the definition of “large load customer” should be changed to contemplate
   the application of the rule on increases of 75 MW or more at a single site within a set time
   period.
        Oncor recommends the Commission revise the definition of “large load customer” in

Section (b)(9) of its second discussion draft so that the large load interconnection standards apply

to a request or requests for an incremental increase or new interconnection of 75 MW or more over

a set time period. The magnitudes of new interconnections and incremental increases are more

relevant to planning standards than the total demand at a given site because the results of resource

adequacy and transmission planning analyses are directly affected by the magnitude of new load

additions. For planning purposes, the impact of interconnecting 20 MW at a site with 60 MW of



ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
Page 5 of 9
 existing peak demand is the same as interconnecting a new 20 MW site nearby; a 20 MW addition

to a 60 MW load, although it results in a total peak demand of over 75 MW at a site, has the same

impact in a resource adequacy or planning analysis as the addition of a new standalone 20 MW

load.

        Grouping all interconnection requests at a given site within a set time period mitigates

gaming of the 75 MW threshold. A customer could not dodge the large load interconnection

standards by requesting a series of repeated under-75-MW interconnection requests. Oncor

recommends a six-year look-back period that would treat any interconnection requests made at the

same site for the previous six years as a single request for the purposes of the 75 MW threshold.

Only the latest under-75-MW incremental request would be studied in the LLIS process.

        To be clear, large load operational standards should apply to all loads with peak demands

over 75 MW because the importance and effectiveness of a large load’s operational response to a

contingency or energy emergency event is proportional to its total demand.

5. Section (k): The capacity reallocation trigger should include an exception for good cause
   delays.
        Oncor reiterates its comments to the first discussion draft, where it recommends that the

Commission modify Section (k) of the discussion draft to give interconnecting utilities discretion

to trigger the reallocation of a large load customer’s unused capacity after the customer fails to

meet a load commissioning plan milestone for 18 months. Oncor recommends that reallocation

be mandatory only after the customer fails to meet its load commissioning plan for 48 months.

This scheme allows flexibility around the capacity reallocation process that will allow utilities to

work with customers who are experiencing reasonable delays in their load commissioning plans

to hold capacity longer.     The current rule is unnecessarily inflexible to reasonable load

commissioning plan delays.

ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
Page 6 of 9
           As an alternative approach, Oncor recommends that the Commission create a good cause

exception to the 18-month reallocation trigger. The interconnecting utility would be required to

notify ERCOT of a customer’s failure to meet a load commissioning plan milestone after 18

months, but the customer could appeal to the Commission for a good cause exception from

reallocation if it is determined that the failure to meet a milestone was the product of a

uncontrollable or unforeseeable delay. This modification to Section (k) would allow for flexibility

in the case of delays caused by factors beyond the large load customer’s control.

                                      II.   CONCLUSION

          Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s evaluations pursuant to Senate

Bill 6.




ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
Page 7 of 9
      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY’S RESPONSE TO
       COMMISSION STAFF’S SECOND RULE 25.194 DISCUSSION DRAFT
   Oncor reiterates its stance on CIAC for system upgrades – interconnecting customers should
    not be responsible for system upgrades because it stifles growth, introduces unnecessary
    complexity, and does not allocate costs based on current or future benefit.
   The initial screening study language should be modified to (i) describe initial study results
    that are clear and realistic and (ii) leave room for a potential initial batch study process.
   The rule should require that, in instances where multiple utilities are involved, they are
    required to execute an agreement or agreements that divide responsibilities amongst the
    utilities.
   The definition of “large load customer” should be changed to contemplate the application of
    the rule on increases of 75 MW or more at a single site within a set time period.
   The capacity reallocation trigger should include an exception for good cause delays.
